$comment: Cross-language signing vectors for the partner notification channel. Produced by disruptions/api/webhook_signing.py and re-derived by disruptions/api/test_webhook_signing.py, so this file cannot drift from the code that signs. Consumed by integrations/notifications-client (TypeScript, via the `standardwebhooks` npm package). Every secret and the root below are TEST VALUES and appear in no deployment.

scheme.name: Standard Webhooks
scheme.signature_header_format: one '<tag>,<signature>' entry per live generation, joined by a single space. A verifier accepts a match on ANY entry, which is what makes each generation independently revocable. Entry order carries no meaning (active first by convention).
scheme.timestamp: whole seconds since the Unix epoch, as a decimal string
scheme.webhook_id: the delivery id: STABLE across every attempt at one delivery, so a receiver may dedupe on it. The timestamp and signature are regenerated per attempt.

derivation.$comment: How a destination's secret is produced, so no signing material is stored anywhere. A partner never needs this -- they are handed the secret -- but an operator reproducing a signature does.
derivation.why_length_framed: a destination id is an operator-supplied string, so ('a', 11) and ('a1', 1) must not share a preimage; a bare separator only holds while no id contains that separator
derivation.secret_format: 'whsec_' + base64(the 32 raw HMAC bytes), standard alphabet, padded

how_to_consume.read_the_body_as: each vector's `body` is a JSON string. UTF-8 encode it to get the exact bytes that were signed, and check it against `body_sha256_hex`. Never re-serialize a parsed object: the signature covers bytes, not a document.

typescript_standardwebhooks.clock_free_check: new Webhook(entry.secret).sign(v.webhook_id, new Date(Number(v.webhook_timestamp) * 1000), v.body) === entry.signature -- sign() takes a Date, so multiply the seconds by 1000. This is the check to run on every vector: it compares byte for byte and consults no clock.
typescript_standardwebhooks.verify_reads_the_wall_clock: Webhook.verify() checks the timestamp against Date.now() and takes no injectable clock, so it CANNOT accept these fixed timestamps. Use it on the `stale-timestamp` vector (expect it to throw) and on messages your test signs itself. Everything else goes through the sign() comparison above.
typescript_standardwebhooks.multi_generation: sign() returns ONE 'v1,...' entry, which is why every vector carries a per-secret `signature` beside the combined `signature_header`. Assert the header equals the verifying entries joined by a single space, in the order given.

how_to_consume.python_reference: webhook_signing.verify(secret=..., webhook_id=..., timestamp=..., body=..., header=..., now=...) -- `now` is injectable, which is how the stale vector is proved to fail for the timestamp rather than for the MAC.

per_secret_fields.secret: the whsec_ value a partner would hold
per_secret_fields.signature: that secret's own 'v1,<base64>' entry over this vector's content
per_secret_fields.verifies: whether this secret must accept `signature_header`. False means it must be rejected -- a revoked generation, or another destination's key.

how_to_consume.verify_at_unix_seconds: the instant to verify AT, so every `verifies` flag below is timeless. For most vectors it is the vector's own `webhook_timestamp`; for `stale-timestamp` it is 301 s later, which is what puts it outside the replay window. Nothing here depends on today's date -- a wall-clock verifier cannot accept any of these fixed timestamps, which is why the sign() comparison above is the check to run.
how_to_consume.mac_is_correct: whether the header's HMAC matches this vector's body, id and timestamp. False only for `tampered-body`. Read it together with `verify_at_unix_seconds`: the two fields are what separate a bad key from a stale timestamp.

vectors.name: plain
vectors.why: The base case. One live generation, a fresh timestamp, an ASCII body. If this vector fails, nothing else in this file will tell you why.
vectors.verify_at_note: its own timestamp, which is inside the 300 s tolerance

vectors.name: retry-same-id-new-timestamp
vectors.why: The SECOND attempt at the same delivery. `webhook_id` is identical to the `plain` vector -- a receiver dedupes on it -- while the timestamp and therefore the signature differ. Reusing the first attempt's timestamp would put a retry outside the 300 s replay window, so a correct receiver would drop our own retry as an attack.
vectors.verify_at_note: its own timestamp, which is inside the 300 s tolerance

vectors.name: rotated-pair
vectors.why: A rotation in progress. The header carries TWO entries, active generation first; each verifies on its own, so either can be revoked without a flag day. A revoked older generation must not verify.
vectors.verify_at_note: its own timestamp, which is inside the 300 s tolerance

vectors.name: cross-destination-isolation
vectors.why: The same message signed for destination A. Destination B's secret for the same generation must NOT verify it: each destination's key is derived from the root over its own id, so one partner's leaked receiver secret forges nothing for another.
vectors.verify_at_note: its own timestamp, which is inside the 300 s tolerance

vectors.name: tampered-body
vectors.why: The header is a VALID signature over a different body (revision 351); the `body` field here is what a man in the middle changed it to (revision 352). Verification must fail. This is also the vector that catches a receiver verifying a re-serialized object instead of the raw bytes.
vectors.verify_at_note: its own timestamp, which is inside the 300 s tolerance

vectors.name: stale-timestamp
vectors.why: The signature is CORRECT over this timestamp -- only the timestamp is old (2026-01-01). So a verifier must reject it for the replay window and not for the MAC, which is what isolates the two failures. Feed this one to a verifier that reads the wall clock: it will stay stale forever.
vectors.verify_at_note: 301 s past its own timestamp -- OUTSIDE the tolerance, which is what this vector tests. `mac_is_correct` is true: verify at `webhook_timestamp` itself and it passes, which is what isolates a replay-window refusal from a wrong-key refusal.
vectors.expected_rejection_reason: the timestamp is outside the 300 s tolerance

vectors.name: norwegian-body
vectors.why: The wording is Norwegian, so the body carries multi-byte characters (æøåÅ, an en dash, an em dash, an arrow) plus an escaped newline. Its UTF-8 byte length and its UTF-16 code-unit length DISAGREE -- see the two length fields -- which is the live failure mode when one side measures or re-encodes the string instead of hashing the UTF-8 bytes. Every character is BMP, so JavaScript's `.length` equals the UTF-16 count and is SMALLER than the byte count; a signature computed over anything but the bytes will not match.

vectors.verify_at_note: its own timestamp, which is inside the 300 s tolerance
